after: ## The relationship between law and morality
alt: Two overlapping circles. Law and morality coincide for murder, rape and theft. Law alone covers morally neutral rules such as which side of the road to drive on or registering a company. Morality alone covers lying to a friend, breaking a non-contractual promise and failing to rescue a stranger. In a pluralist society, laws on disputed issues enforce one group’s view.
caption: Law and morality overlap, but each also covers ground the other does not.

after: ## The relationship between law and morality
alt: Three positions. Natural law (Aquinas): an immoral law is a corruption of law. Fuller’s middle path: law has an inner morality of eight requirements, from being general and public to being applied as announced. Positivism (Austin, Hart): law is valid if made by the recognised process. In the post-war German informer cases Fuller said the laws lacked the qualities of law; Hart said they were law, but wicked.
caption: Natural law builds morality into validity; positivism keeps the two questions apart.

after: ## The legal enforcement of moral values
alt: Three justifications: Mill’s harm principle (prevent harm to others), Devlin’s legal moralism (enforce shared morality, tested by intolerance, indignation and disgust) and legal paternalism (protect people from themselves, partly accepted by Hart). The Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 can be defended as harm prevention or paternalism, or criticised as moralism.
caption: Ask whose harm a law prevents: others’, the person’s own, or none but moral offence.

after: ## The legal enforcement of moral values
alt: R v Brown (1993) upheld convictions for consensual sadomasochistic injuries, supporting Devlin; R v Wilson (1996) quashed a husband’s conviction for branding his wife at her request. Critics say the difference reflects moral judgement about the relationship. Other cases: Knuller v DPP, R v Gibson, Re A (Conjoined Twins) and Nicklinson.
caption: Similar facts, different results: the strongest evidence that courts make moral choices.

after: ## The legal enforcement of moral values
alt: Five responses by Parliament: decriminalising (Sexual Offences Act 1967 after Wolfenden), permitting under conditions (Abortion Act 1967), removing a crime while keeping restrictions (Suicide Act 1961), keeping a prohibition with prosecutorial discretion (DPP consent under section 2), and changing legal recognition (Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013).
caption: Parliament rarely just bans or allows: it often permits under conditions or keeps a discretion.

alt: The annotated paragraph has three moves: link a case to a theory (Brown supports Devlin), add a counter-case and evaluate (Wilson suggests inconsistency), then link to pluralism and reach a judgement (supporting Hart’s harm-based view).
caption: Case and theory, counter-case, then a judgement tied to pluralism.
